content: The composition of intestinal microflora appears to differ between individuals with atopic eczema and those without the condition. These differences in gut microbiota may precede the development of eczema. Probiotics, which are live bacteria that colonize the gastrointestinal tract, are known to provide health benefits to the host. When added to infant feeds, probiotics have the potential to prevent the sensitization of infants to dietary allergens. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effect of administering probiotics to infants for the prevention of allergic diseases or food hypersensitivity. The search strategy included a comprehensive review of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PREMEDLINE, as well as conference abstracts, citations of published articles, and input from expert informants. The selection criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing probiotics to no probiotics, different probiotics to each other, or probiotics with added prebiotics to a control. The quality of the trials was assessed, and data were extracted and synthesized using standard methods established by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria. Six of these studies, involving 2080 infants, assessed outcomes related to allergic diseases and food hypersensitivity, though data were only reported for 1549 infants. The studies generally demonstrated adequate randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of treatment. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution due to significant losses in patient follow-up, ranging from 17% to 61%. A meta-analysis of five studies, which included 1477 infants, revealed a statistically significant reduction in infant eczema (relative risk [RR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 0.95). However, there was considerable heterogeneity among the studies. One study reported that the reduction in eczema persisted until the age of four years. When the analysis was restricted to studies that specifically assessed atopic eczema (confirmed by skin prick tests or specific IgE levels), the findings were no longer statistically significant (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.02). Notably, all studies reporting significant benefits used probiotic supplements containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and enrolled infants at high risk of developing allergies. No other benefits were observed for other allergic diseases or food hypersensitivity outcomes. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine addition of probiotics to infant feeds for the prevention of allergic diseases or food hypersensitivity. While a reduction in clinical eczema was observed in some studies, the effect was inconsistent, and methodological concerns regarding the included studies warrant caution. Further research is necessary to determine whether these findings can be reliably reproduced.
